newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-New drugs keep SmithKline healthy.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-New drugs keep SmithKline healthy.

text.p: Brimming with confidence, Smithkline Beecham on Monday sang the praises of its drugs pipeline, claiming it keeps the Anglo-American company in good shape to go it alone in a merging industry.

Strong sales growth for anti-depressant Paxil/Seroxat is keeping chief executive Jan Leschly happy at the moment, while five new products have entered their final development stages to boost results later this decade.
And to prepare itself for the next century, another group of products, based on genetic research, is scheduled to go into its first clinical trials next year, Leschly said in an interview.
"We have a product portfolio which is comparable to the best in the business," he told Reuters.
"Sometimes I would like to say to analysts: 'do you realise that we have a pipeline that is just as attractive...for half the amount of research as others?'"
SmithKline last week pleased investors with a 14 percent rise in 1996 profits to 1.55 billion pounds ($2.52 billion), but some industry analysts expressed slight reservation.
Their initial enthusiasm was dampened as Leschly said the strength of the pound might rein back earnings growth in 1997.
If the currency stays at its current levels, SmithKline cannot guarantee that double digit growth will continue this year, Leschly said.
"But that should not be a surprise to anyone," he said, adding that adverse currency movements would not affect SmithKline's sound underlying prospects.
"And that is what matters to me and to the shareholders," Leschly said.
He predicted takeover rumours will continue to swirl this year, but reiterated there is no need for SmithKline to join the drugs industry's consolidation process.
"If we will continue to do well and we have double digit growth, why would we need to merge?" he said.
One of the main motors currently driving SmithKline's growth is Paxil, which is rapidly stealing market share from Eli Lilly's blockbuster Prozac.

Leschly expects Paxil sales, which were 706 million pounds last year, to grow by an annual 30 percent in coming years, while the market for new generation anti-depressants is seen increasing by about 20 percent.
Paxil currently has a market share of 21 percent, while Prozac commands about 50 percent and Pfizer's Zoloft controls the remainder.
"But they are losing market share fast and we think we have a drug that is better," said Leschly.
Meanwhile, a handful of new drugs could each generate 300 to 500 million pounds in annual sales if they pass their final tests, he said.
One of the five new medicines targets rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis and asthma.
The other four are intended to fight Alzheimer's disease, type-2 diabetes, migraine and irritable bowel syndrome.
"All very attractive areas to be in," said Leschly.
He also holds great hopes for other new medicines, derived from SmithKline's efforts to crack the genetic code.
SmithKLine established a strong position in genetic research in 1993 when it established a link with Human Genome Sciences which has the world's largest human DNA database.
"It was one of the best deals we ever made," said Leschly. ($1=.6142 Pound)
